(CNN)  -- A fire that claimed the lives of 44 children at a day-care center in Hermosillo, Mexico, started Friday in an air-conditioning unit in an adjacent warehouse, the attorney general of Sonora said Monday. Maria Jesus Coronado Padilla mourns her daughter, Paulette Daniela Coronado Padilla, 2, on Sunday. Investigators have not determined whether the fire was caused by an overheated motor or deficiencies in its installation, said Abel Murrieta Gutierrez, according to the state-run news agency Notimex. However it started, there's no doubt it moved toward papers in bookshelves on the wall shared with the building housing ABC Day Care, where 141 children and day-care workers were, he said. The two buildings also shared a roof, which contained a false bottom made of polyurethane, which overheated, emitting highly toxic fumes, he said. He blamed all 44 of the deaths on the fumes. The general director of the Mexican Institute of Social Security vowed  investigators will pursue the case wherever the evidence takes them. Daniel Karam Toumeh had said Sunday that the building had passed an inspection on May 26. "Here, I want to be very emphatic, in the sense that in Social Security we don't cover for anyone, don't defend anyone, we are the most interested in finding out what it was that happened," he said. As of Monday morning, 20 children ages 1-5 were hospitalized in Hermosillo, and 13 had been taken to other hospitals, including three to Sacramento Shriners Hospital in California, where pediatric burn treatment is a specialty.  Watch parents gather at the site of the fire » . Hermosillo, the capital of the state of Sonora, is about 200 miles (320 kilometers) south of the U.S. border in northwestern Mexico. On a radio show, a firefighter said Monday that many of the children were napping at the time of the fire and died in their sleep. Jose Jesus Diaz, the first firefighter to enter the day-care center, told Radio Los Cheros that he arrived to find some people ramming the building with their vehicles in an effort to reach the children. Inside, Diaz said, he saw children in sleeping positions on the floor. "They never knew what happened," Diaz told the radio station. The scene was one of people crying, calling out names and running with babies, he said. "There's an image that I will carry for the rest of my life: a shirtless man walking outside holding a young boy, yelling 'fireman, fireman, save my son,' but the boy was already dead," Diaz said.  Watch a town in deep shock » . Of the 20 children hospitalized in Hermosillo, 12 were in serious condition. The children taken to Children's Hospital in Sacramento are a 2-year-old boy in serious condition with burns over 20 percent of his body, a 3-year-old boy in critical condition with burns over 50 percent of his body, and a 3-year-old girl in critical condition with burns over 80 percent of her body, a hospital spokeswoman said. CNN's Mariano Castillo in Atlanta and CNN en Español's Rey Rodriguez in Hermosillo contributed to this story.

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — Authorities in Sonora said Monday that the blaze that killed 44 children at a day-care center in Hermosillo, Mexico, began Friday in an air-conditioning unit located in a neighboring warehouse.

On Sunday, Maria Jesus Coronado Padilla grieved for her 2-year-old daughter, Paulette Daniela Coronado Padilla.

Sonora Attorney General Abel Murrieta Gutierrez said investigators had not yet established whether the air-conditioning unit caught fire because its motor overheated or because it had been improperly installed, according to Mexico’s state-run Notimex news agency.

Regardless of the precise cause, Murrieta Gutierrez said the flames spread toward papers stored on bookshelves along the wall that the warehouse shared with the ABC Day Care building, where 141 children and staff members were inside.

The adjoining structures also had a shared roof. According to Murrieta Gutierrez, that roof included a false underside made of polyurethane, which became overheated and released extremely poisonous smoke. He said the toxic fumes were responsible for all 44 deaths.

Daniel Karam Toumeh, director general of the Mexican Institute of Social Security, promised that investigators would follow the evidence wherever it led. He had said Sunday that the facility had passed an inspection on May 26.

“I want to be very emphatic here: in Social Security, we do not protect anyone, we do not defend anyone. We are the ones most interested in discovering exactly what happened,” Karam Toumeh said.

By Monday morning, 20 children between the ages of 1 and 5 remained hospitalized in Hermosillo. Another 13 had been transferred to hospitals elsewhere, including three sent to Sacramento Shriners Hospital in California, a facility known for treating pediatric burn patients.

Hermosillo, the capital of Sonora state, lies in northwestern Mexico about 200 miles, or 320 kilometers, south of the U.S. border.

During a radio interview Monday, a firefighter said many children had been asleep when the fire broke out and died while napping.

Jose Jesus Diaz, the first firefighter to enter the day-care center, told Radio Los Cheros that when he arrived, some people were using their vehicles to smash into the building in an attempt to get to the children.

Once inside, Diaz said, he found children lying on the floor as though they were still asleep.

“They never knew what happened,” he told the station.

He described a scene filled with crying people, parents shouting names, and others running while carrying babies.

“One image will stay with me for the rest of my life,” Diaz said. “A shirtless man was walking outside holding a little boy and shouting, ‘Fireman, fireman, save my son,’ but the boy was already dead.”

Of the 20 children being treated in Hermosillo hospitals, 12 were listed in serious condition.

A spokeswoman for the Sacramento children’s hospital said the three children taken there included a 2-year-old boy in serious condition with burns covering 20 percent of his body, a 3-year-old boy in critical condition with burns over half his body, and a 3-year-old girl in critical condition with burns over 80 percent of her body.

CNN’s Mariano Castillo in Atlanta and CNN en Español’s Rey Rodriguez in Hermosillo contributed to the report.

## Fatal Daycare Center Fire in Hermosillo, Mexico: Background, Cause, Casualties and Eyewitness Accounts

**HERMOSILLO, Mexico** — A fire at the **ABC Daycare Center** in Hermosillo, the capital of the northern Mexican state of **Sonora**, became one of the deadliest child-care disasters in Mexico’s modern history, killing **49 children** and injuring more than 100 others. The tragedy exposed serious failures in building safety, emergency preparedness and government oversight of privately operated daycare centers contracted by Mexico’s social security system.

The blaze broke out on **June 5, 2009**, at the **Guardería ABC**, a daycare center serving children of working parents enrolled in the **Mexican Social Security Institute**, known by its Spanish initials **IMSS**. The center was located in an industrial-commercial area of Hermosillo, a hot desert city near the U.S.-Mexico border and an important manufacturing and government hub in northwest Mexico.

### Location and Background

The daycare was housed in a converted warehouse-like structure in Hermosillo, Sonora. It operated under a model common in Mexico at the time: the IMSS contracted private operators to provide child-care services for the children of insured workers.

The building’s layout later came under intense scrutiny. Investigators and parents said the daycare had inadequate emergency exits, flammable interior materials and structural features that made evacuation difficult. The facility shared walls or close structural proximity with adjoining businesses and storage spaces, including a warehouse linked to the Sonora state government.

For many families, the ABC Daycare Center was a trusted place where infants and young children were left during the workday. On the day of the fire, dozens of children — many of them toddlers and infants — were inside for afternoon rest periods.

### How the Fire Started

The fire began not inside the daycare itself but in an **adjacent warehouse** reportedly used to store documents, vehicle plates or government records associated with the Sonora state finance department. According to official investigations and subsequent reporting, the blaze spread rapidly from that adjoining area into the daycare.

The precise ignition source has been the subject of legal and public dispute. Investigations pointed to an **electrical malfunction or overheating equipment**, with reports focusing on the possibility of a short circuit or an air-conditioning unit in the neighboring warehouse. What is broadly accepted is that the fire spread quickly because of the building conditions and materials in and around the daycare.

Once flames and smoke penetrated the daycare, the situation deteriorated within minutes. Thick toxic smoke filled rooms where children were sleeping or playing. Parents and investigators later said the building lacked adequate emergency exits and that windows were barred or difficult to break, delaying rescue efforts.

### Casualties

The official death toll reached **49 children**. Most were very young, between several months old and around five years old. More than **100 children and adults** were injured, many suffering severe burns, smoke inhalation and long-term respiratory or neurological damage.

Some children died at the scene, while others succumbed later in hospitals in Hermosillo, Guadalajara, Sacramento and other medical centers where the most seriously injured were transferred for specialized treatment.

The high number of victims shocked Mexico and led to days of mourning. Families posted photographs of their children in public vigils, demanding accountability and insisting the deaths were not simply an accident but the result of preventable negligence.

### Survivor and Rescuer Accounts

Survivors, neighbors and rescuers described scenes of chaos as smoke billowed from the daycare and adults desperately tried to reach the trapped children.

Witnesses said bystanders used vehicles, tools and their bare hands to break through walls and windows. Some rescuers reportedly rammed the building with pickup trucks or used sledgehammers and other improvised tools to open holes in the walls after finding doors blocked or insufficient for evacuation.

Parents arriving at the scene encountered a nightmare: smoke, flames, screaming children and rescuers carrying out small bodies covered in soot. Some said they searched frantically at hospitals, moving from one emergency room to another with photographs of their children.

Firefighters and volunteers later recounted that visibility inside the center was nearly zero because of the smoke. Many children were found unconscious from smoke inhalation. Rescuers carried children out in their arms and passed them to waiting ambulances, private cars and pickup trucks because emergency medical resources were overwhelmed.

Some daycare workers were credited by families with trying to save children, while others faced criticism as investigations examined whether evacuation protocols had been followed. Accounts from survivors indicated that the speed of the smoke’s spread made escape extremely difficult, especially for infants and toddlers who could not move on their own.

### Public Outrage and Legal Fallout

The ABC fire triggered nationwide outrage. Parents formed advocacy groups and staged marches demanding justice, arguing that government agencies had failed to enforce safety standards and had allowed a dangerous building to operate as a daycare.

Investigations focused on the daycare’s private owners, local and federal officials, and IMSS administrators responsible for oversight. The case became politically sensitive because some of the daycare’s owners were reported to have ties to influential political families.

Mexico’s Supreme Court later examined the case and found serious violations of constitutional rights related to life, health and child welfare, though the legal consequences for officials and operators were widely criticized by victims’ families as insufficient. Over the years, some individuals faced criminal charges, but many parents continued to say that true accountability had not been achieved.

### Legacy

The Hermosillo daycare fire remains a symbol in Mexico of institutional negligence and the vulnerability of children in poorly regulated care facilities. The families of the victims continue to commemorate the anniversary each year, often using the phrase **“ABC nunca más”** — “ABC never again.”

The tragedy led to renewed scrutiny of daycare safety standards, emergency exits, fire prevention systems and government contracting practices. For the families who lost children or whose children survived with lifelong injuries, however, the fire remains an open wound and a demand for justice that has lasted for years.
